chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: The area of the Republic of Ghana (the then Gold Coast) became known in Europe and Arabia as the Ghana Empire after the title of its Emperor, the Ghana. Geographically, the ancient Ghana Empire was approximately 500 miles (800 km) north and west of the modern state of Ghana, and controlled territories in the area of the Sénégal River and east towards the Niger rivers, in modern Senegal, Mauritania and Mali.

events.label: 10th c.
events.text: Before its fall at the beginning of the 10th century, Akans migrated southward and founded several nation-states around their matriclans, including the first empire of Bono state founded in the 11th century and for which the Brong-Ahafo (Bono Ahafo) region is named.
The empire appears to have broken up following the 1076 conquest by the Almoravid General Abu-Bakr Ibn-Umar.

chapters.narrative: The area of the Republic of Ghana, then the Gold Coast, became known in Europe and Arabia as the Ghana Empire after the title of its Emperor, the Ghana [S1]. Geographically, the ancient Ghana Empire was approximately 500 miles north and west of the modern state of Ghana and controlled territories in the area of the Sénégal River and east towards the Niger rivers, in modern Senegal, Mauritania and Mali [S1]. Before its fall at the beginning of the 10th century, Akans migrated southward and founded several nation-states around their matriclans, including the first empire of Bono state founded in the 11th century and for which the Brong-Ahafo region is named [S1]. The empire appears to have broken up following the 1076 conquest by the Almoravid General Abu-Bakr Ibn-Umar [S1].

chapters.title: Early history
chapters.summary: By the end of 16th century, most of the ethnic groups constituting the modern Ghanaian population had settled in their present locations. Archaeological remains found in the coastal zone indicated that the area had been inhabited since the Bronze Age (ca. 2000 BC), but these societies, based on fishing, had left few traces.

events.label: 9th c.
events.text: The 9th-century Berber historian and geographer Al Yaqubi described ancient Ghana as one of the three most organized states in the region.

events.label: 11th c.
events.text: Ghana succumbed to attacks by its neighbors in the 11th century, but its name and reputation endured.

chapters.narrative: Archaeological remains found in the coastal zone indicated that the area had been inhabited since the Bronze Age (ca. 2000 BC), but these societies, based on fishing, had left few traces [S2]. The 9th-century Berber historian and geographer Al Yaqubi described ancient Ghana as one of the three most organized states in the region [S2]. Ghana succumbed to attacks by its neighbors in the 11th century, but its name and reputation endured [S2]. The forest itself was thinly populated, but Akan-speaking peoples began to move into it toward the end of the 15th century, with the arrival of crops from South-east Asia and the New World that could be adapted to forest conditions [S2]. By the end of 16th century, most of the ethnic groups constituting the modern Ghanaian population had settled in their present locations [S2].

chapters.title: Kingdom of Dagbon
chapters.summary: According to oral traditions and archaeological evidence, the Dagomba states were the earliest kingdoms to emerge in present-day Ghana as early as the 11th century, being well established by the close of the 16th century. Although the rulers of the Dagomba states were not usually Muslim, they brought with them, or welcomed, Muslims as scribes and medicine men.

chapters.narrative: The excerpts provided concern the Kingdom of Dagbon [S3]. According to oral traditions and archaeological evidence, the Dagomba states were the earliest kingdoms to emerge in present-day Ghana as early as the 11th century, being well established by the close of the 16th century [S3]. The excerpts also note that although the rulers of the Dagomba states were not usually Muslim, they brought with them, or welcomed, Muslims as scribes and medicine men [S3]. No other events or details are provided in the currently available excerpts beyond these points [S3].

chapters.title: Bono State
chapters.summary: Bono State (or Bonoman) was a trading state created by the Bono people, located in what is now southern Ghana. It was founded sometime around the eleventh century.

events.label: 12th c.
events.text: The gold trade, which started to boom in Bonoman as early in the 12th century, was the genesis of Akan power and wealth in the region, beginning in the Middle Ages.

chapters.narrative: Bono State (or Bonoman) was a trading state created by the Bono people, located in what is now southern Ghana [S4]. It was founded sometime around the eleventh century [S4]. The gold trade, which started to boom in Bonoman as early in the 12th century, was the genesis of Akan power and wealth in the region, beginning in the Middle Ages [S4]. The available excerpts offer only a concise summary from a single perspective and do not present multiple viewpoints on this history [S4]. No further details regarding daily life, governance, or other events are included in the provided material [S4].

chapters.title: Ashanti Empire
chapters.summary: Under Chief Oti Akenten (r. ca. 1630–60), a series of successful military operations against neighboring Akan states brought a larger surrounding territory into alliance with Ashanti. At the end of the 17th century, Osei Tutu became Asantehene (king of Ashanti).

chapters.narrative: Under Chief Oti Akenten (r. ca. 1630–60), a series of successful military operations against neighboring Akan states brought a larger surrounding territory into alliance with Ashanti [S5]. At the end of the 17th century, Osei Tutu became Asantehene (king of Ashanti) [S5]. By the mid-18th century, Ashanti was a highly organized state [S5]. By the 1820s, successive rulers had extended Ashanti boundaries southward [S5]. The larger surrounding territory was brought into alliance with Ashanti through successful military operations under Oti Akenten [S5]. The extension of boundaries southward by the 1820s followed the earlier organization of the state by the mid-18th century [S5].

chapters.title: Early European contact and the slave trade
chapters.summary: When the first European colonizers arrived in the late 15th century, many inhabitants of the Gold Coast area were striving to consolidate their newly acquired territories and to settle into a secure and permanent environment. events.label: 15th c.
events.text: When the first European colonizers arrived in the late 15th century, many inhabitants of the Gold Coast area were striving to consolidate their newly acquired territories and to settle into a secure and permanent environment.
The Portuguese by 1471 had reached the area that was to become known as the Gold Coast, so named because it was an important source of gold.
The Portuguese interest in trading for gold, ivory, and pepper so increased that in 1482, the Portuguese built their first permanent trading post on the western coast of present-day Ghana.
By 1598, the Dutch began trading on the Gold Coast.
The Dutch built forts at Komenda and Kormantsi by 1612.

events.label: 17th c.
events.text: In the late 17th century, social changes within the politics of the Gold Coast led to transformations in warfare, and to the shift from being a gold exporting and slave importing economy to being a major local slave exporting economy.
The British African Company of Merchants, founded in 1750, was the successor to several earlier organizations of this type.

These nation-states maintained varying alliances with the colonial powers and each other, which resulted in the 1806 Ashanti-Fante War, as well as an ongoing struggle by the Empire of Ashanti against the British, the four Anglo-Ashanti Wars.
In 1807, Britain used its naval power and its diplomatic muscle to outlaw trade in slaves by its citizens and to begin a campaign to stop the international trade.
The importation of slaves into the United States was outlawed in 1808.

chapters.narrative: Many inhabitants of the Gold Coast area were striving to consolidate territories and settle into a secure environment when the first European colonizers arrived in the late 15th century [S6]. The Portuguese reached the area by 1471 and built their first permanent trading post on the western coast of present-day Ghana in 1482 to trade for gold, ivory and pepper [S6]. Initially the Gold Coast did not participate in the export slave trade and the Akan purchased slaves from Portuguese traders from Congo and Benin to augment labour need [S6]. The Dutch began trading by 1598 and built forts at Komenda and Kormantsi by 1612 [S6]. In the late 17th century social changes shifted the economy from gold exporting and slave importing to major slave exporting [S6]. The excerpts reflect a colonial perspective [S6].

chapters.title: British Gold Coast
chapters.summary: By the later part of the 19th century the Dutch and the British were the only traders left. Two major factors laid the foundations of British rule and the eventual establishment of a colony on the Gold Coast: British reaction to the Ashanti wars and the resulting instability and disruption of trade, and Britain's increasing preoccupation with the suppression and elimination of the slave trade.

events.text: The first Ashanti invasion of the coastal regions took place in 1807; the Ashanti moved south again in 1811 and in 1814.

Local British, Dutch, and Danish authorities were all forced to come to terms with Ashanti, and in 1817 the African Company of Merchants signed a treaty of friendship that recognized Ashanti claims to sovereignty over large areas of the coast and its peoples.
In 1823, the First Anglo-Ashanti War broke out and lasted until 1831.
MacCarthy was killed, and most of his force was wiped out in a battle with Ashanti forces in 1824.
The attack, which was launched in January 1874 by 2,500 British soldiers and large numbers of African auxiliaries, resulted in the occupation and burning of Kumasi, the Ashanti capital.
In 1896, the British dispatched another expedition that again occupied Kumasi and that forced Ashanti to become a protectorate of the British Crown.
In 1898 and 1899, European colonial powers amicably demarcated the boundaries between the Northern Territories and the surrounding French and German colonies.
In 1925 provincial councils of chiefs were established in all three territories of the colony, partly to give the chiefs a colony-wide function.

Although political organizations had existed in the British colony, the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC), founded on 4 August 1947 by educated Ghanaians known as The Big Six, was the first nationalist movement with the aim of self-government "in the shortest possible time." It called for the replacement of chiefs on the Legislative Council with educated persons.

This merely established him as a leader and hero, building popular support, and when the first elections were held for the Legislative Assembly under the new constitution during 5–10 February 1951, Nkrumah (still in jail) won a seat, and the CPP won a two-thirds majority of votes cast winning 34 of the 38 elected seats in the Assembly.

chapters.title: Moving toward independence
chapters.summary: In 1945 a Conference (known as the 5th Pan-African Congress) was held in Manchester to promote Pan-African ideas. The Indian and Pakistani independence catalysed this desire.

events.text: In 1945 a Conference (known as the 5th Pan-African Congress) was held in Manchester to promote Pan-African ideas.
Sir Alan Burns' constitution of 1946 established a new legislative council consisting of the Governor as the President, 6 government officials, 6 nominated members and 18 elected members.
Danquah form the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC) in 1947, and Nkrumah was invited to be this party's general secretary.
The electoral victory of the CPP in 1951 ushered in five years of power-sharing with the British.

chapters.narrative: In 1945 a Conference known as the 5th Pan-African Congress was held in Manchester to promote Pan-African ideas, a desire catalysed by Indian and Pakistani independence [S8]. In 1946 Sir Alan Burns' constitution established a new legislative council consisting of the Governor as President, 6 government officials, 6 nominated members and 18 elected members [S8]. In 1947 Danquah formed the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC), and Nkrumah was invited to be this party's general secretary [S8]. The electoral victory of the CPP in 1951 ushered in five years of power-sharing with the British as described in the excerpts [S8].

chapters.title: Independence
chapters.summary: On 3 August 1956, the new assembly passed a motion authorizing the government to request independence within the British Commonwealth. On 18 September 1956 the British set 6 March 1957, the 113th anniversary of the Bond of 1844, as the date that the Gold Coast, Ashanti, the Northern Territories and British Togoland would together become a unified, independent country within the British Commonwealth of Nations under the name Ghana.

events.text: On 3 August 1956, the new assembly passed a motion authorizing the government to request independence within the British Commonwealth.

Nkrumah's regime enacted the Deportation Act of 1957, the Detention Acts of 1958, 1959 and 1962, and carried out parliamentary intimidation of CPP opponents, the recognition of his party as the sole political organization of the state, the creation of the Young Pioneer Movement for the ideological education of the nation's youth, and the party's control of the civil service.
The Second Development Plan of 1959–1964 followed the Soviet model, and shifted away from expanding state services toward raising productivity in the key sectors.
Ghana remained a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy until 1960, when after a national referendum, Ghana was declared a republic.
With the presentation in July 1961 of the country's first austerity budget, Ghana's workers and farmers became aware of and critical of the cost to them of Nkrumah's programmes.

After a bomb attempt on Nkrumah's life in August 1962, Adamafio, Ako Adjei (then minister of foreign affairs), and Cofie Crabbe (all members of the CPP) were jailed under the Preventive Detention Act.
In early 1964, in order to prevent future challenges from the judiciary and after another national referendum, Nkrumah obtained a constitutional amendment allowing him to dismiss any judge.
Other parties having already been outlawed, no non-CPP candidates came forward to challenge the party slate in the general elections announced for June 1965.
Nkrumah had been re-elected president of the country for less than a year when members of the National Liberation Council (NLC) overthrew the CPP government in a military coup on 24 February 1966.
He took up asylum in Guinea, where he remained until he died in 1972.

chapters.narrative: On 3 August 1956, the new assembly passed a motion authorizing the government to request independence within the British Commonwealth [S9]. On 18 September 1956 the British set 6 March 1957 as the date that the Gold Coast, Ashanti, the Northern Territories and British Togoland would together become a unified, independent country within the British Commonwealth of Nations under the name Ghana [S9]. Ghana remained a constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy until 1960, when after a national referendum, Ghana was declared a republic [S9]. Nkrumah had been re-elected president for less than a year when members of the National Liberation Council overthrew the CPP government in a military coup on 24 February 1966 [S9].

chapters.title: Since 1966
chapters.summary: Leaders of the 1966 military coup justified their takeover by charging that the CPP administration was abusive and corrupt, that Nkrumah's involvement in African politics was overly aggressive, and that the nation lacked democratic practices. They claimed that the military coup of 1966 was a nationalist one because it liberated the nation from Nkrumah's dictatorship.

events.text: After a brief period under an interim three-member presidential commission, the electoral college chose as president Chief Justice Edward Akufo-Addo, one of the leading nationalist politicians of the UGCC era and one of the judges dismissed by Nkrumah in 1964.

Leaders of the 1966 military coup justified their takeover by charging that the CPP administration was abusive and corrupt, that Nkrumah's involvement in African politics was overly aggressive, and that the nation lacked democratic practices.
On 15 May 1979, less than five weeks before constitutional elections were to be held, a group of junior officers led by Flight Lieutenant Jerry John Rawlings attempted a coup.
The Constitution entered into force on 7 January 1993, to found the Fourth Republic.
In the presidential election of 2000, Jerry Rawlings endorsed his vice-president, John Atta-Mills, as the candidate for the ruling NDC.
The presidency of Kufuor saw several social reforms, such as the reform in the system of National Health Insurance of Ghana in 2003.
Following the Ghanaian presidential election, 2012, John Dramani Mahama became President-elect and was inaugurated on 7 January 2013.

As a result of the Ghanaian presidential election, 2016, Nana Akufo-Addo became President-elect and was inaugurated as the fifth President of the Fourth Republic of Ghana and eighth President of Ghana on 7 January 2017.
In December 2020, President Nana Akufo-Addo was re-elected after a tightly contested election.
After the Ghanaian presidential election, 2024, John Dramani Mahama was elected as the sixth president of the fourth republic of Ghana and was inaugurated on 7 January 2025.
